cloze.text: Large-diameter instrument handles ({{c1::10 mm}}) provide better {{c2::control}} and decrease {{c3::muscle fatigue}}.
The ideal handle cross-section shape is {{c1::round}}.
A {{c1::hollow}} handle transmits vibrations from the working end to the clinician's fingers.
{{c1::Tapered}} handle ends where the handle is grasped help prevent {{c2::finger slippage}} and require less {{c3::pinch force}} during instrumentation.
Rougher handle surfaces, called {{c1::knurling}}, provide better {{c2::grip}}.
{{c1::Lightweight}} handles put less stress on the hand and fingers while enhancing {{c2::tactile sensitivity}}.
The {{c1::functional}} shank allows the working end to be adapted to the tooth surface.
When the correct working end is used, the {{c1::terminal (lower)}} shank is normally {{c2::parallel}} to the tooth surface being instrumented.
cloze.extra: A helpful visual clue for choosing the correct working end.

cloze.text: {{c1::Longer (extended)}} lower shanks are used in {{c2::deeper pockets}} and posterior teeth.
A {{c1::simple}} shank has only one bend; with the working end facing the clinician, the shank is {{c2::straight}}.
Simple (straight) shanks are used on {{c1::anterior teeth}} and easily accessible areas.
A {{c1::complex (angled/curved)}} shank has multiple bends; with the working-end tip facing the clinician, it has a {{c2::zigzag}} shape.
Complex shanks are commonly used on {{c1::posterior}} teeth; their bends allow access to {{c2::hard-to-reach areas}} and adaptation to bulkier crowns.
cloze.extra: They may also be adapted for anteriors.

cloze.text: Shank flexibility varies with the instrument's task, the {{c1::metal}} used, and the shank {{c2::diameter}}.
{{c1::Thinner, flexible}} shanks allow greater tactile sensitivity; {{c2::thicker, rigid}} shanks allow greater strength.
The {{c1::working end}} is the part of the instrument that does the function, e.g., an explorer tip, a mirror, or blades.
A cutting edge is formed by the junction of the {{c1::face}} and the {{c2::lateral sides}}.
Instruments with two working ends are called {{c1::paired}}; others have only one working end.
The {{c1::cross section}} of a working end determines whether the instrument can be used subgingivally or supragingivally.
Sickle scalers have a {{c1::triangular}} cross-section, a pointed back and {{c2::tip}}, and are used {{c3::supragingivally}} only.
Curettes have a {{c1::semi-circular}} cross-section, a rounded back and {{c2::toe}}, and are used {{c3::subgingivally and supragingivally}}.
Ideal ergonomics — neck: {{c1::centered, minimal bending or rotation}}.
Ideal ergonomics — chin slightly tilted {{c1::down}}, eyes {{c2::15–22 inches}} from the working area.
Ideal ergonomics — shoulders: {{c1::relaxed, neutral}}.
Ideal ergonomics — wrists aligned with hand and forearm, minimal flexion/extension ({{c1::≤15°}}).
Ideal ergonomics — back: {{c1::natural curve}}, minimal torso rotation.
Ideal ergonomics — hips: {{c1::level}} on the clinician's chair.
Ideal ergonomics — knees at a {{c1::105°–125°}} angle from the hips, {{c2::shoulder-width}} apart.
Ideal ergonomics — elbows relaxed, close to the body, bent at {{c1::90°}} at waist level; forearms parallel to the floor; elbows at or above the patient's {{c2::mouth/nose}} level.
Ideal ergonomics — feet {{c1::flat on the floor}}, thighs {{c2::parallel}} to the floor, shoulder-width apart.
The clinician should avoid placing the legs under the {{c1::back of the patient's chair}} (it places the patient too high); legs under the {{c2::headrest}} are acceptable.
Clock positions (figure): for a right-handed clinician, the 'Anterior & Posterior Towards' zone is at {{c1::8–9}} o'clock and 'Posterior Away' at {{c2::10–11}} o'clock.
cloze.extra: Read from the book's clock figure; 'Anterior Away' is at 12 o'clock for both hands.

cloze.text: Clock positions (figure): for a left-handed clinician, the 'Anterior & Posterior Towards' zone is at {{c1::3–4}} o'clock and 'Posterior Away' at {{c2::1–2}} o'clock.
cloze.extra: Mirror image of the right-handed positions; read from the book's clock figure.

cloze.text: In the {{c1::supine}} position, the head, heart, and feet are approximately on the same plane, which reduces the chance of {{c2::syncope (fainting)}}.
The patient's {{c1::tip of the nose}} should always be lower than the clinician's {{c2::elbow}}.
For both maxillary and mandibular treatment, the patient's feet are {{c1::even with or slightly higher than the nose}}.
For maxillary treatment: head aligned with the {{c1::upper end of the headrest}}, chin tilted {{c2::up}}, chair back {{c3::nearly parallel to the floor}}.
For mandibular treatment: head aligned with a {{c1::slightly lowered}} headrest, chin tilted {{c2::down}}, chair back {{c3::slightly raised (15–20°)}}.
The fulcrum finger should be {{c1::strong and stable}} so the instrument can be {{c2::rolled}} easily.
Activate the {{c1::wrist and hand}}, not the fingers, to gain leverage for greater force and lateral pressure and to minimize clinician fatigue.
An {{c1::intraoral}} fulcrum is a finger rest inside the mouth, near the tooth being treated.
An {{c1::extraoral}} fulcrum is a finger rest outside the mouth (e.g., cheek or chin), used in difficult-to-access areas such as {{c2::maxillary posteriors}}.
An {{c1::alternative}} fulcrum is used when an intraoral or extraoral fulcrum is not accessible.
The {{c1::modified pen grasp}} is the recommended grasp for periodontal instruments; it enables precision and control of the working end and reduces {{c2::musculoskeletal injury}}.
In the modified pen grasp the fingers form a soft {{c1::C-shape}} on the handle, allowing the instrument to be rolled to maintain {{c2::adaptation}}.
The {{c1::pad of the middle finger}} is used to feel vibrations (tactile sensitivity).
Modified pen grasp — middle finger: the instrument shank lightly rests on the {{c1::finger pad}}, while the other side touches the {{c2::ring finger}}.
Modified pen grasp — {{c1::index finger and thumb}}: placed opposite each other on the handle; avoid overlapping.
Modified pen grasp — {{c1::ring finger}}: advanced ahead of the other fingers; acts as the {{c2::fulcrum}}.
Modified pen grasp — little finger: kept {{c1::relaxed next to the ring finger}}.
Adaptation: the {{c1::tip (or toe) third}} ({{c2::1–2 mm}}) of the working end is always kept against the tooth to avoid injuring the tissues.
To maintain adaptation as the instrument moves along the tooth, pivot on the {{c1::fulcrum finger}} and {{c2::roll the handle}}.
Angulation is formed between the {{c1::face}} of the instrument and the {{c2::tooth surface}}.
A periodontal probe is positioned {{c1::parallel}} to the tooth surface; in the col it is angled {{c2::20°–30°}} for better access.
Insertion into the sulcus/pocket uses 0°–40° (as flat as possible), allowing {{c1::smooth, atraumatic insertion beneath the gingival margin}}.

Scaling at 45°–90° (ideal 60°–80°) engages calculus effectively; angles less than 45° will {{c1::burnish}} hard deposits, making them difficult to detect and remove and prone to {{c2::plaque biofilm retention}}.
Soft tissue curettage uses an angulation {{c1::greater than 90°}}, directing the cutting edge toward the {{c2::lining of the pocket}} to remove diseased tissue.
Dental hygiene instrumentation uses various {{c1::stroke directions}} to remove deposits and assess tooth surfaces.
A {{c1::vertical}} stroke is parallel to the long axis of the tooth.
Vertical strokes are used on facial, lingual, and proximal surfaces of {{c1::anterior}} teeth and on {{c2::mesial and distal}} surfaces of posterior teeth.
An {{c1::oblique}} stroke is diagonal to the long axis of the tooth; it is used on {{c2::facial and lingual}} surfaces of posterior teeth.
A {{c1::horizontal}} stroke is parallel to the occlusal surface.
Horizontal strokes are used around {{c1::line angles}}, {{c2::furcation areas}}, {{c3::deep pockets}}, and the {{c4::midline of anterior teeth}} — areas where calculus is often missed.
A {{c1::multidirectional}} stroke combines vertical, oblique, and horizontal strokes to ensure complete coverage of all tooth surfaces.
Instrumentation strokes are each designed for a specific purpose, from {{c1::detecting irregularities}} to {{c2::removing deposits}}.
The purpose of the {{c1::assessment/exploratory}} stroke is to detect irregularities and deposits, especially subgingival.
Assessment strokes are {{c1::feather-light}}, long, overlapping, multidirectional, and fluid, with a light grasp and {{c2::no lateral pressure}}.
cloze.extra: Use a light touch on carious lesions.

cloze.text: Assessment strokes are made with the {{c1::probe, explorer, and curet}}.
The {{c1::walking (bobbing)}} stroke advances the probe within the pocket using small {{c2::1–2 mm}} bobbing strokes to avoid tissue trauma.
The {{c1::working (calculus removal/scaling)}} stroke is short, {{c2::biting}}, controlled, and overlapping, with a moderate to firm grasp and {{c3::lateral pressure}} to engage deposits.
Working strokes use vertical, oblique, or horizontal directions; large deposits are removed in sections (called {{c1::channeling}}) to prevent {{c2::burnishing}}.
Working strokes should not be used on {{c1::calculus-free}} surfaces and are followed by an {{c2::exploratory}} stroke to assess removal.
Working (scaling) strokes are made with the {{c1::sickle scaler, universal curet, and area-specific curet}}.
The {{c1::root debridement}} stroke removes plaque and calculus from deep pockets/exposed root surfaces while preserving {{c2::cementum}}.
Root debridement strokes are {{c1::shaving}} strokes with moderate pressure, {{c2::longer}} than calculus-removal strokes, and multidirectional; they are made with an {{c3::area-specific curet}}.
cloze.extra: Avoid excessive cementum removal because cementum is important for healing.

cloze.text: The mirror provides visual access to tooth surfaces and oral structures; a {{c1::fulcrum}} is needed for stability.
The mirror can be used for {{c1::retraction}} of tissues such as the cheek and tongue.
When assessing calculus with an explorer, use the {{c1::side}} of the explorer tip, not the direct tip.
Explorer functions: assessment of calculus, identification of {{c1::tooth anatomy}} (concavities, margins of restorations), and detection of {{c2::carious lesions}}.
Explorer design: a thin working end tapered to a point, {{c1::circular}} in cross section; the last {{c2::1–2 mm}} of the tip is used.
The {{c1::Shepherd's hook (#23)}} explorer is hook-shaped, single-ended, used supragingivally, and best for {{c2::caries detection}} and evaluating restorations.
The Shepherd's hook is too {{c1::thick}} for good tactile sensitivity, and its design prohibits good adaptation in {{c2::pockets or interproximal areas}}.

mcq.question: A hygienist needs to remove calculus 5 mm below the gingival margin. Which working-end design is appropriate?
options: A. Triangular cross-section with a pointed tip
B. Semi-circular cross-section with a rounded toe
C. Circular cross-section tapered to a point
D. Triangular cross-section with a pointed back
mcq.answer: B. Semi-circular cross-section with a rounded toe
mcq.explanation: Curettes (semi-circular cross-section, rounded back and toe) can be used subgingivally. Sickle scalers (triangular, pointed back and tip) are supragingival only — their points would traumatize the pocket. A circular, pointed end is an explorer (assessment, not removal).

mcq.question: Which clinician posture is consistent with ideal ergonomics?
options: A. Wrists flexed about 30° to improve access
B. Elbows held away from the body at shoulder level
C. Knees at a 105°–125° angle from the hips with feet flat on the floor
D. Eyes about 8 inches from the working area
mcq.answer: C. Knees at a 105°–125° angle from the hips with feet flat on the floor
mcq.explanation: Knees 105°–125° from the hips, feet flat, thighs parallel. Wrists should be within ≤15° of flexion/extension, elbows relaxed close to the body at 90° at waist level, and eyes 15–22 inches from the working area.

mcq.question: A patient is being positioned for scaling of the mandibular anterior teeth. Which position is correct?
options: A. Chair back nearly parallel to the floor, chin tilted up
B. Chair back raised 15–20°, chin tilted down
C. Chair back upright at 90°, chin neutral
D. Feet lower than the head, chin tilted up
mcq.answer: B. Chair back raised 15–20°, chin tilted down
mcq.explanation: Mandibular treatment: chair back slightly raised (15–20°), chin tilted down, headrest slightly lowered. Option A is the maxillary position. Feet should always be even with or slightly higher than the nose.

mcq.question: While scaling, a hygienist holds the curet face at about 30° to the tooth surface. The most likely result is:
options: A. Laceration of the pocket lining
B. Burnished calculus
C. Efficient calculus removal
D. Atraumatic insertion beneath the margin
mcq.explanation: Angles below 45° glide over deposits and burnish them, leaving smooth calculus that is hard to detect and retains biofilm. Angles greater than 90° direct the edge into the pocket lining (curettage). 0°–40° is correct for insertion, not for scaling.

mcq.question: Which stroke direction is most appropriate for removing calculus in a furcation area?
options: A. Vertical
B. Oblique
C. Horizontal
D. Walking
mcq.explanation: Horizontal strokes (parallel to the occlusal surface) are used at line angles, furcations, deep pockets and the midline of anterior teeth. Oblique strokes are for facial/lingual surfaces of posteriors; walking is a probing stroke, not a direction.

mcq.question: After removing a ledge of calculus with short, biting strokes, what should the hygienist do next?
options: A. Continue working strokes over the now calculus-free surface
B. Use an exploratory stroke to assess removal
C. Switch to a walking stroke with 50 g of pressure
D. Use a horizontal sickle stroke subgingivally
mcq.answer: B. Use an exploratory stroke to assess removal
mcq.explanation: Working strokes are followed by an exploratory stroke to assess removal; they should not be used on calculus-free surfaces (risk of over-instrumentation and cementum removal). Walking strokes use 10–20 g, and sickles are supragingival.

mcq.question: Which explorer is best suited for detecting caries on occlusal surfaces but poorly suited for subgingival calculus detection?
options: A. Shepherd's hook (#23)
B. Periodontal probe
C. Curet
D. Sickle scaler
mcq.explanation: The Shepherd's hook (#23) is single-ended and supragingival, best for caries detection and evaluating restorations; it is too thick for good tactile sensitivity and cannot adapt in pockets or interproximal areas. The other options are not explorers.
